articles.excerpt_nl: Slimme brillen, kentekencamera’s en deurbellen leggen steeds meer van ons leven vast. Maar niet iedereen loopt hetzelfde risico.
articles.excerpt_en: Smart glasses, licence-plate cameras and doorbells are recording more and more of our lives. But not everyone carries the same risk.
articles.body_nl: Tijdens mijn bachelor liet onze docent ons een korte sciencefictionfilm zien die me nog jarenlang bang zou maken. De film heet [*Sight*](https://www.shortoftheweek.com/2012/07/26/sight). Hij gaat over een man die wakker wordt in zijn lege appartement. In de volgende scène springen zijn augmented-realitylenzen aan en verandert alles. Nu is de kamer helemaal aangekleed. Boven de snijplank zweven recepten en in zijn ooghoeken hangen nieuwsberichten. Zijn lenzen maken van koken een spel met punten en beloningen. De technologie is overal, maar onzichtbaar voor het blote oog. Het wordt pas echt eng wanneer hij een date heeft. Door zijn lenzen staart hij naar de vrouw tegenover hem. Hij ziet niet alleen haar, maar ook informatie over haar. Zij heeft geen idee. In beeld verschijnen aanwijzingen over wat hij moet zeggen, hoe hij moet zitten en wat hij moet bestellen. Het is verschrikkelijk om je eigen keuzes uit handen te geven aan een systeem, zodat je kunt ‘krijgen wat je wilt’. Na de film lag ik nachtenlang wakker. Tot dan toe was surveillance voor mij de overheid die je in de gaten houdt. In geen honderd jaar had ik gedacht dat iemands ogen je stiekem konden filmen en ook nog het gesprek konden sturen. In *Sight* waren de man en zijn lenzen één. Ik weet nog dat ik me afvroeg of dit echt kon gebeuren. Wat als iemand een ruimte binnenloopt en elk gezicht scant op verborgen informatie, zonder dat de ander het ooit te weten komt? Het antwoord kwam sneller dan ik dacht en op de minst spannende manier die je kunt bedenken. In 2024 liepen [twee studenten van Harvard](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/24/technology/facial-recognition-glasses-privacy-harvard.html) met een slimme bril van Ray-Ban en Meta door de metro van Boston. Met PimEyes, een commercieel programma voor gezichtsherkenning, achterhaalden ze wie sommige onbekenden om hen heen waren. Hun video ging viraal. Meta wees er toen op dat de bril een klein wit lampje heeft, zodat mensen kunnen zien dat er wordt gefilmd. Begin 2026 [onthulde The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/13/technology/meta-facial-recognition-smart-glasses.html) dat Meta zelf gezichtsherkenning aan de bril wilde toevoegen, mogelijk al in 2026. Intern heet de functie Name Tag. Via de AI-assistent in de bril zou je mensen kunnen herkennen en informatie over hen krijgen. Meta onderzocht nog wie er herkenbaar zou worden. Dat konden mensen zijn met wie je via een van zijn apps verbonden bent, maar mogelijk ook onbekenden met een openbaar Instagram-account. Iedereen opzoeken zou niet kunnen. Toch komt het akelig dicht bij wat me in *Sight* zo bang maakte. Volgens een intern document dat de krant inzag, overlegde Meta al sinds begin 2025 over een functie met ‘risico’s voor veiligheid en privacy’. In dat memo, van mei 2025, was het bedrijf opvallend eerlijk over de timing. ‘We lanceren in een dynamisch politiek klimaat, waarin veel maatschappelijke organisaties van wie we een aanval zouden verwachten, hun middelen op andere zorgen richten’, staat erin. De politieke onrust in de VS was voor Meta dus juist een goed moment. Aan andere zorgen was geen gebrek. Zo [gebruikt de immigratiedienst ICE gezichtsherkenning](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/30/technology/tech-ice-facial-recognition-palantir.html) op Amerikaanse straten. Democratische Congresleden [vroegen de dienst daarmee te stoppen](https://www.markey.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/letter_to_ice_on_mobile_facial_recognition_tech1.pdf). ‘Gezichtsherkenning op straat vormt een uitzonderlijk ernstige bedreiging voor de praktische anonimiteit waar we allemaal op vertrouwen’, zei Nathan Freed Wessler van de American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) tegen de krant. Name Tag was niet het enige plan. Volgens de krant werkte Meta ook aan een bril die intern ‘super sensing’ heet. Die zou de camera’s en sensoren de hele dag laten draaien en zo een verslag van je dag bijhouden, zoals AI-programma’s een videovergadering samenvatten. Gezichtsherkenning zou daarbij een belangrijke functie zijn, zodat de bril je bijvoorbeeld aan een taak kan herinneren als je een collega ziet. Mark Zuckerberg vroeg zich af of het witte lampje dan aan moet blijven, of dat er een ander signaal komt. In 2024 was dat lampje nog Meta’s antwoord op de zorgen. Nu staat het zelf ter discussie. In *Sight* had de vrouw tegenover de man geen idee. Meta wilde Name Tag eerst uitbrengen op een conferentie voor mensen die blind en slechtziend zijn en pas daarna voor iedereen. Dat is nooit gebeurd. Voor hen kan zo’n bril echt iets betekenen. De directeur van Be My Eyes, een app voor mensen met een visuele beperking, praatte er een jaar met Meta over. ‘Het is zo belangrijk en krachtig voor deze groep mensen’, zei hij tegen de krant. Maar in het memo is de conferentie vooral een opstap naar het grote publiek. Zo wordt toegankelijkheid een schild voor een functie waarvan Meta zelf de risico’s kent. Meta heeft al een geschiedenis met gezichtsherkenning. In 2021 [zette Facebook het systeem stop](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/02/technology/facebook-facial-recognition.html) waarmee gebruikers vrienden op foto’s konden taggen. Het bedrijf betaalde 2 miljard dollar om rechtszaken in Illinois en Texas te schikken, omdat het zonder toestemming gezichtsgegevens had verzameld. In maart 2026 wilden [drie Democratische senatoren](https://www.markey.senate.gov/news/press-releases/markey-wyden-merkley-demand-transparency-from-meta-on-facial-recognition-technology-in-smart-glasses) van Meta weten of het de biometrische gegevens van de bril zou delen met de politie en met het ministerie van Binnenlandse Veiligheid, waar ICE onder valt. Een maand later schreven de ACLU en [75 andere organisaties](https://www.aclum.org/press-releases/aclu-and-75-organizations-sound-alarm-on-metas-plan-to-add-facial-recognition-technology-to-ray-ban-and-oakley-eyeglasses/) een open brief aan Zuckerberg. Met zo’n bril kun je volgens hen de namen achterhalen van mensen bij een demonstratie of een kliniek en die koppelen aan gegevens over hun werk, gezondheid en relaties. Wie daar komt, heeft anonimiteit juist hard nodig. ‘Jouw bril hoort mijn naam niet te kennen’, zei jurist Cody Venzke van de ACLU. Meta liet de krant weten dat het nog over de opties nadenkt en een ‘weloverwogen aanpak’ zal kiezen ‘als en voordat’ het iets uitbrengt. Ondertussen zat de techniek al op miljoenen telefoons. In juni 2026 [onthulde het techblad Wired](https://www.wired.com/story/meta-smart-glasses-face-recognition-nametag-connections/) dat Meta sinds januari stilletjes onderdelen van Name Tag had meegestuurd met updates van de Meta AI-app. Die app is meer dan vijftig miljoen keer gedownload en je hebt hem nodig voor de belangrijkste functies van de bril. Op de telefoons stonden al drie AI-programma’s. Het eerste vindt gezichten in beeld, het tweede snijdt ze uit en het derde zet ze om in een gezichtsafdruk, een unieke digitale code van iemands gezicht. De functie stond nog niet aan. Maar volgens Wired was het systeem zo gebouwd dat de app, zodra de functie aangaat, elk gezicht dat de bril ziet vergelijkt met gezichtsafdrukken op de telefoon. Die verzameling kan Meta vanaf zijn eigen servers aanvullen. Herkent de app iemand, dan krijgt de drager een melding. Alle andere gezichten worden uitgesneden en opgeslagen in een map met de naam ‘pending’, in afwachting dus. In een nieuwere versie van de app heet de functie ‘Connections’, met de belofte dat je ‘de mensen die je ontmoette’ onthoudt. Een onderzoeker testte het systeem met een foto van de Franse filosoof Michel Foucault, die juist schreef over hoe toezicht mensen in bedwang houdt. De app meldde: ‘Person recognized’. ‘Ondanks de miljarden redenen om het niet te doen, lijkt Meta het vermogen te hebben gebouwd om zijn klanten te veranderen in een verspreide surveillancemachine’, zei Cooper Quintin van de digitale burgerrechtenorganisatie EFF tegen Wired. Meta reageerde dat er ‘nog niets is uitgebracht voor consumenten’ en dat er ‘nog geen definitief besluit’ is genomen. Kort daarna [haalde het bedrijf de code weer uit de app](https://petapixel.com/2026/06/09/meta-removes-facial-recognition-code-from-ray-ban-smart-glasses-app/). In september 2026 begonnen ouders en kinderen uit Californië en Illinois [een groepsvordering](https://www.pymnts.com/news/wearables/2026/meta-faces-lawsuit-over-smart-glasses-facial-recognition/) tegen Meta. Ze stellen dat het bedrijf hun foto’s op Facebook en Instagram zonder toestemming gebruikte om Name Tag te ontwikkelen. Meta is niet het enige bedrijf dat zulke berekende keuzes maakt. Lang voordat Meta aan Name Tag werkte, verkochten andere bedrijven al surveillance onder de noemer veiligheid. Een van die bedrijven is Flock Safety. De kentekencamera’s van Flock hangen in de hele Verenigde Staten langs wegen en aan de rand van parkeerplaatsen. Gemeenten haalden ze binnen om gestolen auto’s terug te vinden en criminaliteit aan te pakken. Er kwam nooit een landelijk debat over de vraag of kleine gemeenten wel moesten meedoen aan een groot netwerk dat mensen volgt. Die netwerken zijn in handen van een particulier bedrijf. De lokale politie kan erbij en via de politie ook ICE en de grenspolitie Border Patrol. Pas toen journalisten en onderzoekers de zoekgeschiedenis van Flock in handen kregen, werd duidelijk hoe ver het systeem reikt. [Uit onderzoek van het Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism](https://www.wvtf.org/2025-09-24/vcij-flock-surveillance-ice-immigration-enforcement) uit september 2025 blijkt dat politiediensten het netwerk van Flock in Virginia in één jaar bijna drieduizend keer doorzochten op immigratietermen als ‘ICE’, ‘ERO’ en ‘deportee’. Ongeveer negen op de tien zoekopdrachten kwamen van politiediensten uit andere staten. Een woordvoerder van het sheriffkantoor in Virginia dat het vaakst zocht, bevestigde dat het dat deed als landelijke immigratiediensten erom vroegen. Inwoners dachten dat ze betaalden voor een camera die autodieven zou pakken, maar nu wonen ze in straten die deel uitmaken van een landelijk deportatienetwerk. Het mensenrechtencentrum van de University of Washington vond in de staat Washington minstens acht lokale diensten die hun gegevens lijken te hebben gedeeld met de Border Patrol. In het rapport [*Leaving the Door Wide Open*](https://jsis.washington.edu/humanrights/2025/10/21/leaving-the-door-wide-open/) uit oktober 2025 noemen de onderzoekers dit in feite een ‘voordeur’ voor de landelijke overheid. Op papier bestaat er geen programma voor massasurveillance, en niemand is ervoor verantwoordelijk. Flock [zegt dat het geen contract met ICE heeft](https://www.flocksafety.com/blog/does-flock-share-data-with-ice). De lokale politie zegt dat ze alleen meewerkt aan rechtmatige verzoeken. En de Border Patrol gebruikt alleen wat de gemeente zelf heeft goedgekeurd. Los van elkaar klinkt elk excuus redelijk, en juist daarom is het systeem zo moeilijk aan te vechten. Ring, het deurbelbedrijf van Amazon, gebruikt hetzelfde soort infrastructuur. Maar het bedrijf verkoopt die met een vriendelijker, huiselijker verhaal. In de Super Bowl-reclame van dit jaar komt een weggelopen hond veilig thuis dankzij de functie Search Party. De beelden van de camera’s in de buurt vormen een spoor en uiteindelijk staat de hond voor de juiste deur. Het spotje maakt van een netwerk van bewakingscamera’s iets warms dat buren verbindt. Privacyvoorvechters wezen er meteen op dat een systeem dat is gebouwd om een hond te volgen, net zo makkelijk een mens kan volgen. Ring had ook een samenwerking met Flock Safety gepland. Daardoor zou de politie via Flock beelden van Ring-camera’s kunnen opvragen. Midden in de kritiek op de reclame [blies Ring de samenwerking af](https://abc7news.com/post/ring-flock-partnership-amazon-scraps-surveillance-company-safety-super-bowl-commercial-backlash/18596207/) nog voordat die was begonnen. Ring benadrukte dat er nooit beelden van klanten naar Flock waren gestuurd. Maar de talloze camera’s bleven gewoon draaien. De beelden staan op servers van bedrijven en kunnen later worden doorzocht. Samen laten deze systemen zien hoe technische infrastructuur het leven van gewone mensen vastlegt in een archief. Bedrijven zeggen vaak dat ze gegevens maar kort bewaren. Flock verwijdert kentekens bijvoorbeeld [standaard na een paar dagen of weken](https://www.flocksafety.com/blog/how-does-flock-handle-license-plate-data-deletion). Maar wat de politie in die tijd opslaat of wat online belandt, kan jaren blijven bestaan. Stel je een demonstratie voor in 2024 waar op dat moment bijna niemand van opkijkt. Dan gaan er vier jaar voorbij en komt er een nieuwe regering die een wet verandert of besluit dat een bepaalde groep mensen een probleem is. Nu worden die ‘onschuldige’ beelden van de demonstratie uit 2024 ineens opnieuw bekeken. Niemand hoefde van tevoren te besluiten of die demonstratie gevaarlijk was. Het enige wat nodig is, is dat iemand later een zoekterm intypt en zo de mensen en kentekens tevoorschijn haalt. Mensen zeggen vaak: ‘Wie niets te verbergen heeft, heeft niets te vrezen.’ Dat klopt alleen als de regels nooit veranderen. In Trinidad en Tobago werd seks tussen mannen in 2018 uit het strafrecht gehaald. In 2025 maakte een [hoger hof het weer strafbaar](https://globalvoices.org/2025/03/29/as-trinidad-tobagos-court-of-appeal-reverses-buggery-law-ruling-does-the-colonial-grip-persist/). Omdat het eerst mocht, konden mannen openlijk homoseksueel zijn. Ze liepen mee in de eerste Pride-parade van het land en deelden foto’s online. Die beelden staan er nog. Wie wil, kan nu zien wie er homoseksueel is. Op seks tussen mannen staat weer tot vijf jaar cel. Er wordt zelden iemand vervolgd, maar zulke wetten wakkeren discriminatie, intimidatie en geweld aan. Activist Jason Jones zei na de uitspraak dat het hof ‘[een doelwit op de rug](https://www.thepinknews.com/2025/04/04/trinidad-and-tobago-recriminalises-homosexuality/)’ van lhbtiq+-mensen had gezet. In juli 2026 [behandelde de Privy Council](https://www.guardian.co.tt/news/privy-council-reserves-judgment-in-jason-jones-lgbtqi-rights-appeal-6.2.2622850.8c59a45796) in Londen, de hoogste rechter van Trinidad en Tobago, zijn hoger beroep. Een uitspraak was er bij het schrijven van dit stuk nog niet. Mensen die hebben geleerd dat zichtbaarheid gevaarlijk is in plaats van beschermend, begrijpen dit het best. [Amnesty International onderzocht 21 Europese landen](https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/eur01/8199/2024/en/) en concludeerde dat de vrijheid van meningsuiting en het recht op protest onder druk staan. Amnesty ontdekte dat toezicht op demonstranten angst zaait en mensen ervan weerhoudt naar demonstraties en bijeenkomsten te gaan. [Nederlandse onderzoekers spraken met activisten van Extinction Rebellion](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/20539517241307892). Vooral jonge activisten durven nu minder snel de leiding te nemen. Veel activisten posten minder of helemaal niets meer op sociale media. Onderzoekers noemen dit een ‘chilling effect’. Daarmee bedoelen ze het moment waarop iemand aarzelt om nog iets te doen, alleen omdat die zich bekeken voelt. De zorg om opgepakt te worden is al erg genoeg. Nog erger is het besef dat een of ander bedrijf gegevens over je bewaart buiten elke democratische controle. Je weet niet wat dat bedrijf heeft bewaard of wanneer het weer opduikt. Het werk van de Amerikaanse socioloog Ruha Benjamin maakt duidelijk dat dit gevaar niet met de smartphone begon. Surveillance is altijd een manier geweest om mensen onder controle te houden. Onderzoekers die surveillance bestuderen, zeggen al jaren dat het niet iedereen op dezelfde manier treft. Nieuwere technologie versterkt oude vormen van controle meestal, in plaats van ze te vervangen. In haar boek *Race After Technology* introduceert Benjamin de term ‘New Jim Code’, naar de Jim Crow-wetten die in het zuiden van de VS rassenscheiding voorschreven. Ze bedoelt daarmee technologie die neutraal of zelfs vooruitstrevend kan lijken, maar witte mensen als de norm neemt en mensen van kleur benadeelt. In plaats van openlijke rassenscheiding zit het vooroordeel nu ingebouwd in algoritmes en scoresystemen. Die bepalen wie een huis of lening krijgt en wie door de politie in de gaten wordt gehouden of kansen misloopt. Ook in Nederland is dit geen theorie. In de toeslagenaffaire gebruikte de Belastingdienst nationaliteit als aanwijzing in een systeem dat aanvragen voor kinderopvangtoeslag automatisch als risicovol markeerde. [De Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens noemde dat](https://nos.nl/artikel/2340965-toezichthouder-werkwijze-belastingdienst-discriminerend-en-onrechtmatig) in 2020 onrechtmatig en discriminerend. Duizenden ouders werden ten onrechte als fraudeurs behandeld en moesten soms tienduizenden euro’s terugbetalen. Een parlementaire commissie sprak in december 2020 van ‘[ongekend onrecht](https://www.parlement.com/kabinetscrisis-2021-kinderopvangtoeslagaffaire)’ en een maand later trad het kabinet-Rutte III af. [Volgens het CBS](https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/maatwerk/2022/48/actualisatie-uithuisplaatsingen-toeslagenaffaire-2015-t-m-juni-2022) werden tussen 2015 en medio 2022 ruim tweeduizend kinderen van gedupeerde ouders uit huis geplaatst. Of dat door de affaire kwam, heeft het CBS niet onderzocht. De cijfers over fouten bij gezichtsherkenning zijn te hoog om te negeren. Volgens een [test uit 2019 van het Amerikaanse standaardinstituut NIST](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2019/NIST.IR.8280.pdf) waren verschillende commerciële systemen minder nauwkeurig bij het herkennen van zwarte vrouwen en Aziatische mensen dan bij witte mannen. In het onderzoek [Gender Shades](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v81/buolamwini18a.html) uit 2018 testten Joy Buolamwini en Timnit Gebru systemen die het geslacht van een gezicht moesten bepalen. Bij vrouwen met een donkere huid zaten die er tot bijna 35 procent van de keren naast, bij mannen met een lichte huid in minder dan 1 procent. Een gezicht dat de machine als wit en mannelijk ziet, levert bijna nooit problemen op. Bij vrouwen met een donkere huid werkt gezichtsherkenning te vaak simpelweg niet. Het systeem verwart hen vaker met iemand anders en soms herkent het hun gezicht helemaal niet. Vooral pijnlijk is dat ze als een probleem worden gezien in plaats van als een mens. Benjamin heeft er een naam voor: ‘coded exposure’. Daarmee bedoelt ze dat technologie zwarte mensen tegelijk slecht ziet en extra in de gaten houdt. Het is makkelijk om het een glitch te noemen en het op te lossen met een paar zwarte programmeurs en betere trainingsdata. Maar Benjamin waarschuwt juist voor dat idee: vooroordelen behandelen als ‘een ongelukkige glitch in de verder neutrale ontwikkeling van technologie’. Het is geen fout. Het is, in haar woorden, ‘een signaal van hoe het systeem werkt’. De software staat niet op zichzelf. PredPol was bijvoorbeeld een van de meest gebruikte systemen voor voorspellend politiewerk in de VS. Het was gebaseerd op een model dat oorspronkelijk naschokken van aardbevingen moest voorspellen. Elke dag vulde PredPol een raster op de kaart met kleine rode vlakjes, op basis van oude misdaadcijfers. Die cijfers gaan vooral over plekken waar de politie was geweest. Het systeem stuurde de politie terug naar dezelfde straten. Hoe meer politie er is, hoe meer aanhoudingen en arrestaties er komen. Die worden dan gezien als bewijs dat het systeem gelijk heeft. Zoals Benjamin schrijft, zal software die zulke data gebruikt ‘de politie altijd eerder naar buurten sturen zoals die waarin ik ben opgegroeid’. Het hele uitgangspunt wordt dus bepaald door vooroordelen in de data. De machine herhaalt ze sneller en op grotere schaal dan agenten op straat ooit zouden kunnen. De onderzoeker Simone Browne laat de patronen zien van surveillance en controle waaronder zwarte mensen leefden. In *Dark Matters* bestudeert ze de verschillende middelen die het makkelijker maakten om mensen onder slavernij en koloniaal bewind te controleren. Ze schrijft over de plattegrond van het slavenschip Brookes, waarop alle tot slaaf gemaakte mensen dicht op elkaar getekend staan. Met gloeiende ijzers werden ze gebrandmerkt als bezit van hun eigenaar. Ook advertenties voor gevluchte tot slaaf gemaakten laten dat zien. Mensen waren daarin niet meer dan een korte beschrijving van hun brandmerken en littekens. In New York verplichtten de zogeheten lantaarnwetten tot slaaf gemaakte mensen boven de veertien om na zonsondergang een lantaarn met een brandende kaars bij zich te dragen. Dat gold voor zwarte en inheemse mensen en voor mensen van gemengde afkomst. Zo kregen ze nooit de kans om ongezien door de stad te gaan. In 1784 klaagde een anonieme briefschrijver in een New Yorkse krant over de wreedheid van deze wet. Een witte dronkaard mocht tot middernacht ongestraft de straat op stelten zetten, stond in de brief, terwijl een zwart meisje van vijftien bij wie de wind de kaars uitblies, naar de gevangenis werd gebracht en de volgende ochtend in het openbaar werd gegeseld. Met deze wetten en andere praktijken ontstond een wereld waarin zij zich nooit voor de staat konden verbergen. Richt de politie nu een camera met gezichtsherkenning op een menigte in de stad, dan doet ze wat ze altijd al heeft gedaan. Alleen is het gereedschap nu nieuw. Benjamin en Browne beschrijven allebei een vergelijkbare tweedeling. Sommige mensen moeten te volgen zijn, waar ze ook gaan. Anderen lopen door dezelfde straten zonder een spoor achter te laten. En als het systeem een fout maakt, zijn de gevolgen heel echt. Een verkeerde match kan leiden tot een [onterechte arrestatie](https://www.clickondetroit.com/tech/2024/06/28/detroit-paying-300000-to-man-wrongly-accused-of-theft-making-changes-in-use-of-facial-technology/), een baan die je zonder uitleg misloopt of een aanhouding die gevaarlijk wordt. Het kan zelfs een mensenleven kosten. Het gaat niet alleen om het foutpercentage, maar ook om de vraag wie überhaupt in de gaten wordt gehouden. De systemen zijn gericht op zwarte gemeenschappen, moslimgemeenschappen, ongedocumenteerden, activisten, sekswerkers en queer- en transpersonen in een vijandig politiek klimaat. Zij zijn de eersten op wie surveillance wordt getest en worden het hardst getroffen. Name Tag, Flock en Ring stellen de vraag: wie mag ongezien blijven? Er zijn nog steeds mensen die door een stad bewegen zonder een digitaal spoor achter te laten. Ze kunnen meelopen in een demonstratie zonder dat hun kenteken in een politiedatabase belandt. Ze zijn niet bang dat de deurbelcamera van de buren hen filmt op weg naar het ziekenhuis. Ze kunnen ontspannen in een café zitten zonder zich zorgen te maken dat iemand hun gezicht scant. Maar sommige mensen worden aan de andere kant van die scheidslijn geboren. Surveillance wordt meestal gezien als iets wat mensen van buitenaf wordt opgelegd. Wat we vaak over het hoofd zien, is dat wij zelf die camera’s kopen en aan onze deur hangen. Dragen we straks een bril die de hele dag meekijkt, dan leggen we iedereen om ons heen vast. Zelfs wie de bril niet herkent, belandt in een map die ‘pending’ heet. Flock-camera’s in je straat en Ring-beelden die in de buurtapps worden gedeeld, helpen een archief op te bouwen dat de wetten van nu kan overleven. De strijd tegen surveillance gaat verder dan wetten en systemen achter de schermen. Hij zit ook in onze gewoontes. Die verandering is niet voor iedereen gelijk. Mensen die al nauwlettend in de gaten worden gehouden door de politie of hun buren, merken het als eersten. Voor hen is die zichtbaarheid bijna nooit neutraal geweest. articles.body_en: When I was an undergraduate, our professor showed us a short sci-fi film that scared me for years. The name of the film was *[Sight](https://www.shortoftheweek.com/2012/07/26/sight)*. It was about a man who woke up in his empty apartment. In the next scene, his augmented‑reality contact lenses come to life, changing the room completely. Now his room is fully decorated. We see recipes floating above the chopping board, news reports hovering at the periphery of his vision, and his lenses have turned his cooking into a game with points and achievements. The technology is everywhere, but invisible to the naked eye. It takes a dark turn when he goes on a date. He stares at the woman across from him through the lenses. Now, with the help of those lenses, he can see her and her information, but she has no idea. The prompts guide him, telling him what to say, how to sit, and what to order. It is truly terrible to lose the ability to make decisions on your own and allow the system to make them on your behalf so that you can “get what you want”. After the screening, I couldn’t sleep for nights. When I was growing up, I connected surveillance with the government watching you. Never in a million years did I think it could be built into someone’s eyes, secretly recording and dictating the conversation you share. Well, in *Sight*, the device and the man were one. I remember wondering whether this was a possibility. What if someone could walk into a room and scan every face for hidden data, without the other person ever knowing? The answer came sooner than I thought, and in the least exciting way possible. In 2024, [two Harvard students](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/24/technology/facial-recognition-glasses-privacy-harvard.html) walked through the Boston subway wearing Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses. Using PimEyes, a commercial facial recognition program, they found out who some of the strangers around them were. Their video went viral. Meta pointed out at the time that the glasses have a small white light, so people can see when they are being filmed. In early 2026, *[The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/13/technology/meta-facial-recognition-smart-glasses.html)* [revealed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/13/technology/meta-facial-recognition-smart-glasses.html) that Meta itself wanted to add facial recognition to the glasses, possibly as soon as 2026. Internally, the feature is called Name Tag. Through the AI assistant in the glasses, you would be able to recognise people and get information about them. Meta was still working out who would be recognisable. That could be people you are connected to through one of its apps, but possibly also strangers with a public Instagram account. It would not be able to look up everyone. Still, it comes uncomfortably close to the thing that had scared me about *Sight*. According to an internal document seen by the paper, Meta had been discussing the feature since early 2025 and identified “safety and privacy risks,” but the discussion then turned to the question of when to launch. The memo, from May 2025, was strikingly honest about the timing. “We will launch during a dynamic political environment where many civil society groups that we would expect to attack us would have their resources focused on other concerns,” it reads. So for Meta, the political turmoil in the United States presented an opportunity rather than an obstruction. There was no shortage of other concerns. ICE, for example, [uses facial recognition](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/30/technology/tech-ice-facial-recognition-palantir.html) on American streets. Democratic lawmakers [asked the agency to stop](https://www.markey.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/letter_to_ice_on_mobile_facial_recognition_tech1.pdf). “Face recognition technology on the streets of America poses a uniquely dire threat to the practical anonymity we all rely on,” Nathan Freed Wessler of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) told the paper. Name Tag wasn’t the only plan. According to the paper, Meta was also working on glasses internally called “super sensing.” They would keep the cameras and sensors running all day and keep a record of your day, the way AI programs summarise a video meeting. Facial recognition would be a key feature, so the glasses could, for example, remind you of a task when you see a colleague. Mark Zuckerberg wondered whether the white light should then stay on, or whether there should be a different signal. In 2024, that light was still Meta’s answer to people’s concerns. Now the light itself is up for debate. In *Sight*, the woman across from the man had no idea. Meta wanted to launch Name Tag at a conference for blind and low-vision people first, and only then release it to everyone else. That never happened. For them, glasses like these could genuinely make a difference. The CEO of Be My Eyes, an app for people with visual impairments, spent a year talking to Meta about it. He told the paper how important and powerful it could be for this group of people. But in the memo, the conference is mostly a stepping stone to the wider public. That is how accessibility becomes a shield for a feature whose risks Meta itself knows. Meta already has a history with facial recognition. In 2021, Facebook [shut down the system](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/02/technology/facebook-facial-recognition.html) that let users tag friends in photos. The company paid \$2 billion to settle lawsuits in Illinois and Texas for collecting face data without consent. In March 2026, [three Democratic senators](https://www.markey.senate.gov/news/press-releases/markey-wyden-merkley-demand-transparency-from-meta-on-facial-recognition-technology-in-smart-glasses) asked Meta whether it would share biometric data from the glasses with the police and the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE. A month later, the ACLU and [75 other organisations](https://www.aclum.org/press-releases/aclu-and-75-organizations-sound-alarm-on-metas-plan-to-add-facial-recognition-technology-to-ray-ban-and-oakley-eyeglasses/) wrote an open letter to Zuckerberg. They cautioned that integrating facial recognition technology into consumer glasses would make it much easier to identify strangers at protests or outside clinics, and to link their names to data about their work, health and relationships. In these places, anonymity is extremely important to people seeking safety and protection. “Your glasses should not know my name,” said ACLU senior staff attorney Cody Venzke. A Meta spokesperson said the company was “still thinking through options” and would take “a thoughtful approach if and before” it rolled anything out. Meanwhile, the technology was already on millions of phones. In June 2026, [the tech magazine](https://www.wired.com/story/meta-smart-glasses-face-recognition-nametag-connections/) *[Wired](https://www.wired.com/story/meta-smart-glasses-face-recognition-nametag-connections/)* [revealed](https://www.wired.com/story/meta-smart-glasses-face-recognition-nametag-connections/) that since January, Meta had quietly been shipping parts of Name Tag in updates to the Meta AI app. The app has been downloaded more than 50 million times, and you need it for the glasses’ main features. Three AI programs were already on the phones. The first finds faces in an image, the second crops them out, and the third turns them into a faceprint, a unique digital code of someone’s face. The feature was not switched on yet. But according to *Wired*, the system was built so that once the feature is turned on, the app compares every face the glasses see with faceprints on the phone. Meta can add to that collection from its own servers. If the app recognises someone, the wearer gets a notification. All other faces are cropped and saved in a folder called “pending.” In a newer version of the app, the feature is called “Connections,” with the promise that you can “remember the people you met.” A researcher tested the system with a photo of the French philosopher Michel Foucault, who wrote about how surveillance keeps people in line. The app reported “Person recognized.” Meta “seems to have created the capacity to turn their customers into a distributed surveillance machine,” Cooper Quintin of the digital rights group EFF told *Wired*. Meta responded that “nothing has shipped to consumers” and that “no final decision has been made.” Shortly afterwards, the company [removed the code from the app](https://petapixel.com/2026/06/09/meta-removes-facial-recognition-code-from-ray-ban-smart-glasses-app/). In September 2026, parents and children from California and Illinois filed [a class action](https://www.pymnts.com/news/wearables/2026/meta-faces-lawsuit-over-smart-glasses-facial-recognition/) against Meta. They claim the company used their Facebook and Instagram photos without permission to develop Name Tag. Meta is not the only company making calculated decisions like this. Long before Meta’s glasses existed, other companies were already selling surveillance under the banner of safety. One of them is Flock Safety. Its automated licence-plate readers stand along roads and at the edges of parking lots in the United States. Towns brought them in to recover stolen vehicles and respond to crime. There was no national debate about whether small towns should join a larger, networked tracking system. Those networks are owned by a private company. Local police can search them, and through the police, so can ICE and the Border Patrol. Journalists and researchers figured out the full scale of it once they received Flock’s query logs. According to [a September 2025 investigation by the Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism](https://www.wvtf.org/2025-09-24/vcij-flock-surveillance-ice-immigration-enforcement), almost three thousand searches were made in a year on Flock’s network in Virginia. In those searches, police were using terms related to immigration, such as ‘ICE,’ ‘ERO,’ and ‘deportee.’ Roughly 9 out of 10 searches were made by police departments in other states. A spokesperson for the Virginia sheriff’s office that made the most searches confirmed that it did so when federal immigration authorities asked it to. People who believed they were paying for a camera that would catch car thieves are living on streets that have become part of a national deportation net. The University of Washington Center for Human Rights found at least eight local agencies in Washington state that appear to have enabled data-sharing with the US Border Patrol. In the report *[Leaving the Door Wide Open](https://jsis.washington.edu/humanrights/2025/10/21/leaving-the-door-wide-open/)*, published in October 2025, the researchers describe the set-up as effectively a “front door” to federal access. On paper, there is no mass-surveillance program, and no one is responsible for it. Flock will tell you that [it has no contract with ICE](https://www.flocksafety.com/blog/does-flock-share-data-with-ice). Local police say they respond only to lawful requests. And the Border Patrol is only using tools the town agreed to. Individually, each excuse makes sense, which is exactly why it’s so hard to fight. Amazon’s Ring uses the same kind of infrastructure. But it is being sold with a nicer, more homey story. This year’s Super Bowl ad shows a lost dog returning home safely with the help of the Ring “Search Party” feature. Using the neighborhood’s cameras, a trail of clips is woven, and at last, the dog appears at the right door. It presents networked surveillance as something warm and communal. Privacy advocates were quick to point out that the system built to track the dog could also easily track a person. Ring had also planned a partnership with Flock Safety that would permit police using Flock to request footage captured by Ring cameras. Amid the backlash to the ad, [Ring ended the partnership](https://abc7news.com/post/ring-flock-partnership-amazon-scraps-surveillance-company-safety-super-bowl-commercial-backlash/18596207/) before it even started. Ring emphasised that no customer footage had ever been sent to Flock. But countless cameras were still operating. Their footage is stored on company servers and can be searched later. Taken together, these systems show how technical infrastructure builds archives of ordinary lives. Companies often say they only keep data for a short time. Flock, for example, deletes licence-plate data [after a few days or weeks by default](https://www.flocksafety.com/blog/how-does-flock-handle-license-plate-data-deletion). But whatever the police save in that time, or whatever ends up online, can stick around for years. Imagine a march in 2024 that hardly raises an eyebrow at the time. Then, four years pass, and a new administration comes into power and either changes a law or decides that a given group of people is a problem. Now those “innocent”-looking images from the 2024 march suddenly get a second look. No one had to decide ahead of time whether the 2024 march was dangerous. All that needs to happen is for someone later to type a term into a search box and pull up the people and license plates. People often say, “Nothing to hide, nothing to fear.” This is only true if the rules never change. Sex between men was decriminalised in Trinidad and Tobago in 2018, but it was later [recriminalised by a higher court in 2025](https://globalvoices.org/2025/03/29/as-trinidad-tobagos-court-of-appeal-reverses-buggery-law-ruling-does-the-colonial-grip-persist/). Because it was allowed at first, men could be openly gay. They marched in the country’s first Pride parade and shared photos online. Those images are still there. Anyone who wants to can now see who is gay. Sex between men carries up to five years in prison again. Prosecutions are rare, but laws like this fuel discrimination, harassment, and violence. After the ruling, activist Jason Jones said the court had “[effectively put a target on the back of LGBTQIA+ people](https://www.thepinknews.com/2025/04/04/trinidad-and-tobago-recriminalises-homosexuality/).” In July 2026, [the Privy Council](https://www.guardian.co.tt/news/privy-council-reserves-judgment-in-jason-jones-lgbtqi-rights-appeal-6.2.2622850.8c59a45796) in London, Trinidad and Tobago’s highest court of appeal, heard his appeal. At the time of writing, it had not yet ruled. People who have learnt that visibility is dangerous rather than protective understand this best. [Amnesty International looked at 21 European countries](https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/eur01/8199/2024/en/) and found that freedom of expression and the right to protest are under threat. It discovered that surveillance of protesters creates fear and deters people from attending demonstrations and meetings. [Dutch researchers spoke with activists from Extinction Rebellion](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/20539517241307892). Young activists in particular are now more hesitant to take the lead. Many activists post less on social media, or have stopped altogether. Researchers have labelled this a “chilling effect,” referring to the moment when a person hesitates to act at all just because they feel watched. The fear of being arrested is bad enough. Even worse is knowing that some company is storing data about you beyond any democratic control. You don’t know what it has kept or when it might come back to haunt you. The work of American sociologist Ruha Benjamin makes it clear that this danger did not start with smartphones. Surveillance has always been a technology of control. For years, people in surveillance studies have been saying that not everyone is affected by it in the same way. Newer tools mostly reinforce old technologies of control rather than replace them. In her book *Race After Technology*, Benjamin introduces the phrase “New Jim Code,” after the Jim Crow laws that enforced racial segregation in the American South. She uses it to describe technologies that may appear neutral or even progressive but take white people as the default and disadvantage people of colour. Instead of clear segregation, bias is now built into algorithms and scoring systems, determining who gets housing, who receives credit, and who is subject to policing or denied opportunities. In the Netherlands, this is not just theory either. In the childcare benefits scandal, the Dutch Tax Administration used nationality as an indicator in a system that automatically flagged applications for childcare benefits as high-risk. In 2020, [the Dutch Data Protection Authority called this](https://nos.nl/artikel/2340965-toezichthouder-werkwijze-belastingdienst-discriminerend-en-onrechtmatig) unlawful and discriminatory. Thousands of parents were wrongly treated as fraudsters, and some had to pay back tens of thousands of euros. In December 2020, a parliamentary committee spoke of “[unprecedented injustice](https://www.parlement.com/kabinetscrisis-2021-kinderopvangtoeslagaffaire),” and a month later the Rutte III cabinet resigned. [According to Statistics Netherlands (CBS)](https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/maatwerk/2022/48/actualisatie-uithuisplaatsingen-toeslagenaffaire-2015-t-m-juni-2022), more than two thousand children of affected parents were placed in out-of-home care between 2015 and mid-2022. CBS did not investigate whether the scandal was the cause. The figures for facial recognition errors are too high to be overlooked. According to [a 2019 test by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2019/NIST.IR.8280.pdf), several commercially sold systems were less accurate at identifying Black women and Asian people than white men. In the 2018 [Gender Shades](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v81/buolamwini18a.html) study, Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested systems that had to determine the gender of a face. For women with darker skin, they got it wrong up to almost 35 per cent of the time; for men with lighter skin, less than 1 per cent of the time. A face read by the machine as white and male almost never creates any trouble. Too often, it quite simply does not work for women with darker skin. It is more likely to mix them up with someone else, and at times it just doesn’t see their face at all. What is particularly painful is that they are seen as a problem instead of human beings. This tendency even has a name: “coded exposure.” Benjamin uses it to describe how technology both fails to see Black people and watches them more closely. It’s easy to call it a glitch and fix it with a few Black engineers and better training data, but Benjamin warns against this very concept: treating bias as “an unfortunate glitch in the otherwise neutral development of technology.” It isn’t a bug. In Benjamin’s words, it is “a kind of signal of how the system operates.” The software doesn’t exist on its own. For example, PredPol was one of the most widely used predictive-policing systems in the US. It was based on a model originally built to forecast aftershocks following earthquakes. PredPol then filled map grids with tiny red boxes every day, based on old crime data. The crime data is mainly about the places the police went to. It took the police back to the same blocks. The more police there are, the more stops and arrests there will be, which are then seen as proof that the system is right. As Benjamin writes, software using this kind of data “will always be more likely to direct police to neighborhoods like the one I grew up in.” The whole premise is therefore ruled by bias in the data, and the machine repeats it faster and to a greater extent than any patrol work could. Simone Browne demonstrates the patterns of surveillance and control that Black people lived under. In *Dark Matters*, she studies the different tools that made it easier to control people under slavery and colonial rule. She writes about the floor plan of the slave ship Brookes, where every enslaved person was packed in and mapped out before the journey. Hot irons were pressed into their skin so they could be branded as the property of their owners. Runaway slave advertisements were further evidence, reducing people’s existence to short descriptions of their individual marks and scars. One of the regulations, called the lantern laws, compelled enslaved Black, mixed-race and Indigenous New Yorkers over the age of fourteen to carry a lantern with a lit candle after sunset, so that they would never have the chance to move through the city unseen. In 1784, an anonymous letter writer in a New York newspaper complained about the cruelty of these laws. A “white drunkard” could “disturb the street til midnight, with impunity,” the letter said, while “a poor black girl of fifteen” whose candle was blown out by the wind “is hurried to gaol, and next morning ignominiously scourged in public.” These were the laws and other practices that led to a world where people were never hidden from the state. Today, when the police direct a facial recognition camera at a crowd in the city, they are doing what they have done for as long as they have existed, except that they now have a new engine. Benjamin and Browne are both characterising a similar divide. Some people are meant to be traceable wherever they go. Others move through the same streets without leaving a trace. And when the system makes a mistake, the stakes aren’t hypothetical. A wrong match can mean [a wrongful arrest](https://www.clickondetroit.com/tech/2024/06/28/detroit-paying-300000-to-man-wrongly-accused-of-theft-making-changes-in-use-of-facial-technology/), a job denied without an explanation, or a stop that turns dangerous. It could even cost a life. This isn’t just about the error rate, but about the question of who gets watched in the first place. The systems are aimed at Black and Muslim communities, undocumented people, activists, sex workers, and queer and trans people in hostile political climates. They are the first people on whom surveillance is tested, and they are hit the hardest. Name Tag, Flock, and Ring ask: Who gets to stay unseen? There are still people who can move through a city without leaving a digital record. They can join a protest without having their car’s license plate recorded in a police database. They have no fear of a neighbor’s doorbell camera capturing them on their way to the hospital. They can relax at a bar without worrying that someone might scan their face. But some people are born on the other side of that divide. Surveillance is generally seen as an external imposition on people. What we often overlook is that we are the ones buying cameras and attaching them to our doors. When we wear glasses that watch all day long, we record everyone around us. Even the people the glasses don’t recognise end up in a folder called “pending.” Flock cameras on your street and Ring clips shared on neighbourhood apps help build an archive that might outlast today’s laws. The surveillance fight now goes beyond back-end systems and laws. It enters our habits. This change is not equal for all people. The individuals already watched minutely by the police or their neighbours are the most affected. This visibility has almost never been neutral for them. It makes them more likely to be stopped today, and their data will still be on file when the rules change. ## Sources ACLU of Massachusetts (2026, April 13). Sinds de doorbraak van non-fungible tokens — kortweg NFT's — in 2021 is er een verhaal in omloop dat klinkt als een belofte. De technologie zou digitale kunstenaars eindelijk de mogelijkheid geven om hun werk te verkopen zonder tussenkomst van galeries, veilinghuizen of de traditionele poortwachters van de kunstwereld.

Het klinkt utopisch. En precies daarom is het de moeite waard om er een stap dichterbij te kijken.

## De onderzoeksvraag

In mijn thesis stel ik de vraag: hoe verhoudt het NFT-project *Reloading* — een samenwerking tussen ART X Lagos en het NFT-platform SuperRare — zich tot dekoloniale narratieven die gekleurd worden door blockchain-imaginaries? Anders gezegd: wat doen Afrikaanse kunstenaars met deze technologie, en wat doet de technologie met hen?

## Wat blockchain wel en niet doet

Een van de meest taaie misverstanden over blockchain is dat het inherent decentraal zou zijn. Dat is afhankelijk van het soort blockchain. *Permissionless* blockchains zijn open voor iedereen. *Permissioned* blockchains hebben poortwachters, en het zijn juist die laatste die door overheden en grote bedrijven worden omarmd.

## Wat blijft hangen

Wat ik aan deze thesis heb overgehouden is geen conclusie maar een methode. De vraag is niet *"is deze technologie goed of slecht?"*. De vraag is: welke machtsverhoudingen lopen er op dit moment door deze technologie heen, wie heeft daar baat bij, en wie wordt erin gevangen?

*An excerpt from my master's thesis at the University of Amsterdam, New Media & Digital Culture, 2022.*

Since the breakthrough of non-fungible tokens — NFTs for short — in 2021, a story has circulated that sounds like a promise. The technology would finally allow digital artists to sell their work without intermediaries — without galleries, auction houses, or the traditional gatekeepers of the art world.

It sounds utopian. Which is exactly why it's worth looking closer.

## The research question

In my thesis I ask: how does the NFT project *Reloading* — a collaboration between ART X Lagos and the NFT marketplace SuperRare — engage with decolonial narratives coloured by blockchain imaginaries? In other words: what are African artists doing with this technology, and what is the technology doing to them?

## What blockchain does and doesn't do

One of the stickiest misunderstandings about blockchain is that it is inherently decentralised. That depends on the kind of blockchain. *Permissionless* blockchains are open to everyone. *Permissioned* blockchains have gatekeepers — and it is precisely the latter that governments and large corporations have embraced.

## What stays with me

What I took from this thesis is not a conclusion but a method. The question is not *"is this technology good or bad?"*. The question is: which power relations are currently running through this technology, who benefits, and who is caught in it?

---

*Deze essay is gepubliceerd in het Engels. Schakel rechtsboven naar EN voor de volledige tekst, of lees hieronder.*

---

*This essay is part of an ongoing series of living research. It exists both on paper and in practice. I invite your reflections, questions, and disagreements, and hope it can be a space where dialogue continues beyond the page.*

I did not begin this work inside institutions. As a student, I was part of a grassroots initiative that set out to decolonise the curriculum. We worked with universities, museums, and other organisations, but I was wary of being on the inside. I did not believe that change could come from within the very structures that produced the problem. Years later, when I joined a large, self-described progressive organisation, I saw how familiar that logic was: colleagues spoke passionately about justice and equality, but the organisation remained centred on white, highly educated norms. The gap between its public commitments and its internal life was impossible to ignore.

In many large, self-described progressive organisations — from NGOs to universities and cultural institutions — diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) have become part of the organisational moral self-image. Its importance is woven into the organisation's public life, from the way it describes itself in official documents to the way it presents itself in recruitment and external communication. On the surface, there is often broad agreement that inclusion, representation, and equity matter. What is striking, however, is how rarely this rhetorical agreement translates into the kinds of structural changes that DEI, in its most serious sense, actually demands. Because the question is never only about who is present, but whose voices carry authority, how power is distributed, and what forms of experience and knowledge are allowed to count as expertise. In Patricia Hill Collins's terms, the struggle over inclusion is also a struggle over epistemic authority: whose standpoint is treated as a legitimate source of knowledge, and whose insights remain marginal or conditional (Collins, 2019). The contradiction reveals itself clearly when inclusion shifts from being a mere statement of intent to a required action that organisations must undertake. Embracing diversity as a principle is a relatively easy endeavour. Inclusion transforms into a complex challenge when it transcends rhetorical affirmation in words, demanding instead an actual institutional change. This rarely encounters outright rejection. What unfolds, however, is more straightforward. It is uncommon for individuals to express a direct refusal. Across different organisations, the responses are remarkably consistent. Inclusion remains a concept that is celebrated in theory, yet its actualisation is perpetually deferred.

There is a particular kind of meeting in which this dynamic plays out almost predictably. Here, the community actively participates in ethical conversation, and everyone acknowledges the importance of equity and fairness. But the moment inclusion begins to imply the redistribution of power, the room begins to tighten up. It is not that anyone explicitly says no. Instead, they often show their reluctance by being hesitant rather than outright refusing. After that, you'll notice that the discussion slows down and becomes more careful. In one organisation where I worked, this took the form of repeated objections whenever racial justice and leadership were raised. Proposals to centre race in strategy were met with worries about "losing our current base" or "alienating supporters," and suggestions to appoint more leaders of colour were blocked with familiar phrases: "we can't find the right candidates," "we need someone now." An external DEI bureau was eventually brought in, but their work focused on gossip and interpersonal tensions rather than the structural conditions that made people of colour feel unheard. The discomfort of white colleagues became the main object of concern, while the experiences of people of colour were further sidelined. What began as a subject of structural change evolves into a question of tone, procedure, and how to conduct the conversation appropriately. In these situations, inclusion is still validated, but only if it does not disrupt what has already been established. The institution can accommodate diversity as a desire more easily than as a requirement. The focus shifts from what needs to change to how change might be communicated without unsettling those who are most accustomed to being comfortable. At that point, the limits of the institution's commitment become visible.

As Sara Ahmed reminds us, this resistance is not always loud or identifiable, but it is structural, sedimented in what she calls the brick wall of institutional life. Diversity practitioners often describe their work as "banging your head against a brick wall," a phrase Ahmed uses to theorise how institutions exert their own kind of passivity. The wall is not necessarily built out of open hostility but out of habit, repetition, and what she calls the "background ease" of institutional life. This is the sense that things already make sense as they are. Diversity work, then, becomes work against the grain of institutional automatisms, work that makes visible what the institution has naturalized as "just how we do things here." The more persistently practitioners push for change, the more tangible the wall becomes; the institution reveals its friction precisely when challenged to act differently (Ahmed, 2012, pp. 23–27). This is exactly the institutional mechanism Ahmed theorises in *On Being Included* (2012).

Ahmed describes diversity commitments as "non-performatives": meaning statements that express a desire to act ethically but fail to translate that intention into action (Ahmed, 2012, pp. 16–18). Rather than serving as a catalyst for changing an institution's actions, commitment transforms into a fundamental aspect of the institution's self-description. So, you see, DEI is not absent but absorbed. Instead of being a force that compels the institution to change, it becomes proof that the institution is good. Ahmed makes more than just the claim that institutions are dishonest. It is much more unsettling than that. The institution can take up the terminology of critique without actually allowing critique to do its work. DEI becomes institutional language, even while practitioners continue to experience the institution as resistant to their labour (Ahmed, 2012, pp. 16–18). As Ahmed puts it, the paradox is that diversity becomes omnipresent as an official language at the very moment practitioners encounter the institution as immovable. The very fact that organisations hire diversity officers, set up committees, and produce policy documents can become a sign of this paradox. Practitioners are told to "make diversity a goal", which is already an indication that diversity is not yet an institutional given. The hiring of a diversity officer may even signal the absence of broader support, as if the organisation can claim legitimacy by simply having someone "just there" (Ahmed, 2012, p. 22). This helps explain why DEI so often becomes concentrated in the domain of communication and symbolism. Not necessarily because individuals inside organisations are cynical, but because institutions govern themselves through risk, reputation, and continuity. NGOs, in particular, rely on moral legitimacy. Their survival depends on donors, partnerships, stakeholder confidence, and public trust. In that context, it makes institutional sense to speak the language of inclusion. Silence is costly, and so is speaking incorrectly. But adopting the right language is comparatively inexpensive, so long as it does not become a binding demand for the redistribution of power. Here, an important contrast between inclusion as performance and inclusion as governance becomes apparent. Performance is about how an organisation presents itself and how it gets an ethical image. While governance relates to the structure of power: who decides, who takes charge, how resources are distributed, what constitutes professionalism, how institutional norms are perpetuated, and which accountability systems are really important. A lot of institutions are prepared to spend money on performance. Far fewer are willing to pursue governance-level transformation because governance change always involves the issue of who must give up comfort, power, or prestige.

The frequent appeal to the "business case" for diversity often highlights this contradiction. In institutional discourse, the business case refers to the idea that inclusion is not only morally desirable but also has economic advantages. DEI is justified in terms of performance, innovation, profitability, and organisational resilience rather than justice alone. In the last ten years, the discourse surrounding consultancy reporting and management research has consistently drawn upon this argument. McKinsey's influential reports, *Diversity Matters* (2015), *Delivering Through Diversity* (2018), and *Diversity Wins* (2020), draw on large datasets of more than 1,000 companies across different regions and sectors, and they identify a clear correlation between leadership diversity and the likelihood of financial outperformance. While it is important to acknowledge that these results are correlational and not strictly causal, they have increasingly been treated as central to the dominant narrative that inclusion is beneficial both ethically and practically (McKinsey & Company, 2015, 2018, 2020). At the same time, critical scholars have warned that the "business case" can be fragile. Mike Noon, for example, argues that pinning equality to commercial returns risks undermining it: if the numbers no longer support a performance gain, the moral claim to justice becomes easier to discard (Noon, 2007, pp. 773–775).

In this instance, it is crucial to recognise that the presence of evidence does not cancel out the existence of resistance. Considering that diversity holds both moral significance and practical benefits, what accounts for the ongoing resistance within institutions? In most cases, a lack of data is not the answer. The answer always lies in power. Organisational strength may be correlated with diversity, but forms of dominance that are not easily surrendered are threatened by the redistribution of that power. While an institution may reap advantages as a whole, certain groups may see inclusion as a threat to their unwritten standards, such as the status quo, the influence of familiarity with the culture, or the ease with which one may define professionalism according to one's own image. For this reason, DEI initiatives so often collapse into training programmes: workshops, listening sessions, mandatory modules. Training is not meaningless, but it is institutionally appealing because it relocates the problem to the realm of interpersonal sensitivity and individual attitudes. It creates the appearance of movement without requiring structural confrontation. Organisational research has long been sceptical of such approaches when they are not paired with accountability mechanisms. Frank Dobbin and Alexandra Kalev, for example, draw on three decades of data from more than 800 U.S. firms and hundreds of interviews with managers to show that many standard diversity programmes fail precisely because they do not change the systems through which organisations hire, promote, and assign responsibility, and that mandatory training can even generate backlash rather than durable change (Dobbin & Kalev, 2016, pp. 53–58). One of the clearest expressions of institutional resistance is the persistent claim that "there are not enough qualified candidates" from underrepresented groups. Scarcity is rarely the real issue. The real problem is recognition. Leadership is reproduced through cultural codes that appear neutral but are not, through informal expectations about what authority sounds like, where competence is assumed to reside, and who is trusted without explanation. Diversity becomes acceptable so long as it does not disrupt these norms. Difference may be welcomed, but transformation is not.

This institutional pattern is not confined to Anglo-American contexts. Similar dynamics, shaped by local histories and norms, appear in Dutch organisational life as well. In *Leiderschap in Kleur*, Judi Mesman draws on qualitative interviews with forty leaders of colour in the Dutch (semi-)public sector to describe what she calls "white standards and expectations": the persistent pressure to adapt to prevailing institutional norms in environments that offer little space for difference on its own terms (Mesman, 2022, pp. 2–3). Participants describe a double burden. They are expected to lead, while simultaneously having to navigate otherness, misunderstanding, and a lack of support from above, becoming in Nirmal Puwar's terms "space invaders": bodies that enter spaces historically reserved for white, male norms, whose very presence exposes how those spaces were never neutral to begin with (Mesman, 2022, p. 3; Puwar, 2004). Mesman also points to how organisations can use a small number of leaders of colour to suggest that the problem has been solved, even when underlying norms and structures remain largely unchanged, turning representation into a form of tokenism rather than shared responsibility for change. Mesman's conclusion is blunt in its simplicity: diversity and inclusion are not achieved by placing a single person of colour in a leadership position. Without mandate, shared responsibility, and structural change in organisational culture, representation becomes another form of isolation (Mesman, 2022, p. 4).

What emerges, then, is not primarily a story of individual malice, but a structural one. Institutions can present themselves as inclusive while remaining organised around inherited hierarchies. Diversity becomes less a redistribution of power than a form of institutional virtue, something the organisation can point to as evidence of goodness. As Audre Lorde puts it, "the master's tools will never dismantle the master's house": practices that leave the underlying structures intact may offer recognition or comfort, but they do not alter the terms on which power is organised (Lorde, 1984, p. 112). The organisation remains largely the same, even as the vocabulary of inclusion expands around it. Inclusion is welcomed, but only as long as it does not require the institution to change how power actually works.

---

## References

Ahmed, S. (2012). *On Being Included: Racism and Diversity in Institutional Life.* Durham, NC: Duke University Press.

Collins, P. H. (2019). *Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory.* Durham, NC: Duke University Press.

Dobbin, F., & Kalev, A. (2016). Why diversity programs fail. *Harvard Business Review,* 94(7–8), 52–60.

Lorde, A. (1984). The master's tools will never dismantle the master's house. In *Sister Outsider: Essays and Speeches* (pp. 110–114). Freedom, CA: Crossing Press.

McKinsey & Company. (2015). *Diversity Matters.* McKinsey & Company.

McKinsey & Company. (2018). *Delivering Through Diversity.* McKinsey & Company.

McKinsey & Company. (2020). *Diversity Wins: How Inclusion Matters.* McKinsey & Company.

Mesman, J. (2024). *Leiderschap in kleur: Ervaringen van mensen van kleur in leiderschapsposities in de (semi-)publieke sector.* Leiden: Universiteit Leiden / Algemene Bestuursdienst.

Noon, M. (2007). The fatal flaws of diversity and the business case for ethnic minorities. *Work, Employment and Society,* 21(4), 773–784.

Puwar, N. (2004). *Space Invaders: Race, Gender and Bodies Out of Place.* Oxford: Berg.

---

This essay began, as many things in my life do, with a conversation with my best friend while I sat in a café. Neither of us have children, but we found ourselves talking about how we would want to raise them: what it might mean to teach a child that mistakes are survivable and that being held to account does not have to mean being cast out. As we talked, I thought about the times we had lost and found each other again and again after conflict.

Relationships have never been a neutral topic for me. I grew up in a house where love did not arrive alone. Danger sat at the same table, punishment was ordinary, and a child learnt early that safety could vanish without warning. In that world, being wrong did not mean "I made a mistake." It meant "I might not survive this."

For years, that training came with me into every relationship I touched. Before anyone else could punish me, I did it myself, convinced that if something went wrong it must be my fault, that something in me was rotten. In the same breath, I punished others when they hurt me. Someone who disappointed me became a villain in my mind. When conflict appeared, I disappeared. I cut contact and found it almost impossible to stay open. No one had ever shown me how to do that.

Healing did not begin as a noble wish to become a better person. It began as a survival project, a question of how to stay alive in myself and how to function at all. My story is only one version of this, yet it rests inside a larger pattern. Many of us brace ourselves as soon as accountability enters the room. The words arrive dressed as punishment. What begins as "you did something harmful" is heard as "you are harmful," and "this behaviour must change" turns into "your character is on trial." Under those conditions, even necessary confrontation can feel like annihilation. Therefore, defensiveness, denial, and self-justification are not mysterious responses. They belong to people who have been taught, again and again, that wrongdoing makes them unworthy of belonging.

She calls us toward a love ethic, toward an understanding of love as practice, woven from care, commitment, responsibility, respect, trust, and knowledge. Taking that seriously means accepting responsibility for how we show up with one another and letting love be measured by what we do rather than by what we claim to feel. Many of us have learnt to hear "we need to talk" as the start of rejection, humiliation, or control rather than a chance to deepen the relationship. We pull back in whatever way we can. In close relationships, people cut each other off rather than staying in contact long enough to work through what happened. In political life, harm is turned into a public drama that creates shame and headlines while very little actually changes. Online, the same habits are amplified. People are cast out with a few posts or comments, and the speed of reaction leaves almost no space for nuance, reflection, or repair. Even the way many adults speak to children passes on the same lesson: that making a mistake means you are the problem.

Studies of parent-child relationships suggest that shame and guilt do not work in the same ways. Harsh, punitive environments are linked to stronger and more damaging shame responses, while warmer and more supportive relationships make it easier for children to recognise wrongdoing without collapsing into worthlessness. Shame goes after the self. Guilt, when it is taken seriously in a caring relationship, can turn a child's attention toward impact and repair. Where shame freezes, hides, and attacks back, guilt held in a trusting relationship can open a doorway to empathy and connection. A child who is repeatedly addressed as if they are the problem does not learn to do better. They learn to be vigilant, avoidant, or highly skilled at defence. Raising children with integrity means holding a fierce line on behaviour while protecting, just as fiercely, their sense of being worthy of love and belonging. The face across the table may be fully grown, but the reaction comes from much earlier, from the part of a person that learnt love could be withdrawn at the first sign of failure. In that sense, much of the resistance to accountability is not resistance to truth but to humiliation, exile, or emotional collapse. The act of denying responsibility becomes a means of maintaining one's integrity when accountability has always been seen as an attack.

None of this should be seen as a justification for engaging in harmful behaviours. Still, the damage is significant. However, taking harm seriously also means asking how defensiveness was learnt and how it protects people from feeling the full weight of what they have done. Work in restorative justice is helpful here because it shifts the question. Instead of asking only who is guilty and how they should be punished, the focus turns to what happened, who was affected, and what repair is needed. In many circles, that practice is literal. People sit together in the same room and speak about impact, responsibility, and what needs to change so that the same harm does not repeat. The point is not to erase what happened, but to face it together and decide what repair is possible. This sort of accountability is not more lenient; rather, it simply is more demanding of each and every person in the room.

When harm is met with punishment, people often learn to act sorry without being genuinely touched. They grow quiet, say what they think is expected, play the part of remorse, and wait for the storm to pass. Nothing in the relationship has to change. Loving accountability asks for something harder. It stays with what happened and with its impact until both people can feel the weight of it. In that space, the person is always more than the harm, and the harm is acknowledged because the person matters. These truths are held together. You try to keep faith with the person while still saying, as clearly as you can, that what they did cannot continue.

The actual work starts now, developing through conversation and focused attention. The focus shifts toward understanding the impact of what has happened, while holding responsibility in a way that does not collapse into self-hatred or punishment. Change takes shape gradually, as patterns of interaction are reworked and something more intentional begins to guide the way you meet each other. What sustains it is a steadiness that neither hardens into judgement nor slips into neglect. Care becomes deliberate, shaped by boundaries that make continued connection possible. From within that clarity, the future is no longer assumed but slowly reimagined, carried by a language that can hold both truth and attachment at once.

Instead of reading someone's character, attention returns to what actually happened. The relationship becomes the starting point, making it possible to speak from care for what exists between you and a belief that something more honest can take shape. The tone changes as accusations like "you always" or "you are" begin to fall away. What replaces them is a more grounded way of speaking, one that stays close to experience, names impact, and makes room for change. Softer language does not dilute the truth; it removes some of the theatre of shame and opens space for accountability that can be lived rather than performed.

To hold each other in this way asks for vulnerability from the one who raises the issue. Calling someone in with love means acknowledging that it matters enough for silence to feel like abandonment. The discomfort of honesty is chosen over the false peace of keeping everything inside. There is care in that choice, and there is risk. Love, in this sense, is not simple reassurance but a willingness to enter conflict without letting it become a reason to end the relationship.

The person who is called in also has work to do. In a punitive culture, the first impulse is often to protect your sense of self at any cost, and that protection can quickly become another way of avoiding responsibility. A different kind of listening is needed. Accountability can be heard not as a verdict on who you are, but as information about what you did and what it did to someone else. You might notice your defensiveness while still recognising the other person's perspective, or acknowledge that harm was caused regardless of intent. At times, it means asking for space to think so that you can respond rather than react. These are not ways of proving innocence, but of staying in the conversation long enough for something other than reflex to emerge, allowing guilt to move toward reflection instead of collapsing into shame.

When it comes to accountability, a love-based practice has to work on both sides. The one who names harm is asked to resist the pull of punishment, including the lure of superiority and the desire to win. This requires stepping away from simple stories with clear villains and victims, and from the satisfaction of feeling justified within them. The task is to remain with what actually happened, without turning the other person into a symbol.

The one who is called in faces a different demand. It involves turning away from defensiveness, denial, and the impulse to retreat into self-victimisation, as well as letting go of the idea that good intentions cancel out harm. Staying present long enough to hear the impact can feel almost unbearable, yet it is part of the work. Both people are being asked to step outside the familiar logic of guilt and to trust, at least in part, that discomfort can move something rather than only wound it. This is difficult because punishment often presents itself as seriousness; what looks like moral clarity can feel like the only responsible response, especially when harm is still raw. This is less about scripting every argument and more about establishing, before anything erupts, that conflict is expected, that care does not depend on perfection, and that everyone involved intends to stay accountable when things become difficult.

At the same time, they come to understand that actions have consequences, and that repair is part of living with others rather than an occasional performance after a crisis. Being held to account then becomes one of the ordinary ways love appears, not a sign that love is being withdrawn.

On a larger scale, institutions face their own version of this challenge. Many swing between bureaucratic punishment and vague therapeutic language, either turning harm into a file or dissolving it into abstraction. A more consistent form of rigour would mean building cultures where feedback, consequence, and growth can exist together in public and predictable ways, so that people know what happens when harm is named. In such places, harm is neither treated as an individual flaw to be expelled nor as something to be smoothed over, but taken up as a shared responsibility that calls for attention, learning, and, as far as possible, repair.

No set of practices removes the pain. Even at its most careful and loving, accountability still grazes the ego and touches places we would rather leave in the dark. To be called in, or to call someone else in, means agreeing to meet ourselves where we would rather not look. That encounter hurts. The point is not to deny that hurt or dress it up as growth, but to separate it from punishment. Pain is not automatically a sign that we are being cast out or condemned. Sometimes it is the feeling of a relationship insisting on truth, refusing the comfort of denial or pretending. Sometimes it is the ache of knowing that something more honest is being asked of us, that a different way of being together has become nonnegotiable.

The hardest work does not end with our own reactions. It is also cultural. Many of us have been trained to believe that being confronted means we are no longer loved, and that confronting someone else means becoming cruel. Those lessons run deep. They keep people away from the conversations that might allow relationships to change instead of quietly decay. Yet both stories are false.

A more demanding truth is that accountability can be one of the most tender forms of regard. To hold someone to account with love is to say, in words or in actions, that this mattered, that you still matter, that what happened cannot be swept aside, and that there is still a path, if you are willing to walk it, toward something better than denial or disappearance. That path is rarely smooth. It asks for courage, patience, and a tolerance for ambiguity. The difficulty is not a sign that love has failed. It is often the clearest sign that love is being taken seriously.
